title: Multi-omics machine learning prioritizes a plasma lipid signature for active tuberculosis differentiation
summary: Machine-learning integration of plasma functional-omics data in two discovery cohorts and a validation cohort identified biosignatures that distinguished active tuberculosis from nontuberculous mycobacterial infection, latent TB infection and other lung diseases. Cohorts included 76 people in the TB–NTM discovery set, 72 in the TB–LTBI–other-lung-disease set, and 68 TB plus 30 LTBI participants in the validation set. PC(14:0_22:6) was the most important predictor and was lower in active TB; additional external datasets yielded reported AUCs of 0.77–1.00.
ai_technology: Multi-omics integration and machine-learning predictive models for feature selection and classification
organization: Inje University College of Medicine; Ton Duc Thang University; Hanoi University of Pharmacy; University of Copenhagen; Korea University Guro Hospital

evidence.tested: Machine-learning integration of plasma functional-omics data in two discovery cohorts and a validation cohort identified biosignatures that distinguished active tuberculosis from nontuberculous mycobacterial infection, latent TB infection and other lung diseases.
evidence.unknown: The article calls PC(14:0_22:6) a candidate differential-diagnostic biomarker. Reported AUCs vary by comparator group and dataset; they do not establish prospective performance, clinical utility, or replacement of microbiological diagnosis. The PubMed abstract does not provide all cohort-level assay details, so this summary remains bounded to abstract-reported information.
evidence.ai_role: The authors used machine-learning predictive modeling across integrated functional-omics measurements to identify and prioritize plasma signatures that discriminate active TB from clinically relevant non-TB groups. PC(14:0_22:6) emerged as the leading lipid feature; the analysis was evaluated across discovery, validation and two external datasets.
